title: Mockito unit tests
summary: Control a dependency’s response while checking a real service.

sources.title: Engineering Digest: Mockito Spring Boot Tutorial | @Mock @InjectMocks

richText: Replace a dependency with a mock
A mock is a replacement object controlled by the test.
Use a mock for a dependency such as a repository when checking a service’s decisions.
The service under test stays real. A mock repository does not connect to the database.
@Mock creates a mock field.
@InjectMocks creates the object under test and attempts to inject its mock dependencies.
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) prepares Mockito for JUnit Jupiter.
Set responses and check results
Stubbing sets the response a mock should return. Use when(...).thenReturn(...).
An assertion checks the service’s result or exception.
verify(...) checks whether a particular call was made to the mock.

example.title: Return a stored title or report a missing entry
description: The Titles dependency returns an Optional containing a title, or an empty Optional for a missing entry.
explanation: Mockito creates the Titles mock and injects it into TitleService.
The first test makes the repository return Morning for entry-1.
assertEquals checks the returned title. verify checks the requested entry ID.
The second test returns an empty Optional and checks that the service throws IllegalArgumentException.
Neither test starts Spring or calls a database.

richText: Arguments and failures
Use exact arguments when the value is part of the behavior being checked.
A matcher such as anyString() accepts many values. Use it only when the exact value does not matter.
If one argument uses a matcher, use matchers for every argument in that call. eq(value) matches a specific value.
ArgumentCaptor records an argument passed to the mock so the test can check its fields.
Use doThrow(...).when(mock).operation(...) to simulate an exception from a void method.
What a Mockito test does not load
@InjectMocks does not apply Spring transactions, security filters or configuration.
A plain @Mock field does not replace a bean in a Spring application context.
Use a database integration test to check real queries or transaction rollback.
